6.3 Active vs. Passive Investing

4.7 The Efficient Market Hypothesis and 4.9 Performance Evaluation discussed active management from the viewpoint of market efficiency and performance evaluation. This lesson takes the viewpoint of a household choosing funds: the logic of the active-versus-passive debate, the evidence, and how to read fund documents.

The arithmetic of active management

Section titled “The arithmetic of active management”

Passive investing holds the whole market weighted by market capitalization (index fund); active management tries to earn more than the market by picking stocks or timing the market.

Sharpe (1991) pointed out a simple fact. Divide all investors into two groups: passive investors hold the market portfolio, so before costs they earn exactly the market return; all investors together hold the market portfolio, so active investors as a group can also earn, before costs, only the market return. Writing RMR_MRM​ for the market return and cAc_AcA​ for the average cost of active management, weighted by money:

RˉA=RM−cA\bar{R}_A = R_M - c_ARˉA​=RM​−cA​

Wins and losses among active investors are zero-sum: if some beat the market, others must lag it. Since active management costs more (fees, trading costs) than passive investing, after costs the average active dollar must lag the average passive dollar. This conclusion does not depend on whether markets are efficient, only on the definition of an average (Exercises Question 1).

Check C1
If there are enough active managers and they are clever enough, active investors as a group can beat the market after costs.
What do active and passive investors hold together? What do passive investors earn before costs? What, then, do active investors as a group earn before costs?

The SPIVA evidence

Section titled “The SPIVA evidence”

S&P Dow Jones Indices publishes the SPIVA reports twice a year, comparing active funds with matching indexes. The reports have two features: funds that were liquidated or merged along the way are included and counted as not beating the index; and each category of funds is compared with an index of its own style. According to the SPIVA U.S. Scorecard (year-end 2024):

Fund category (benchmark)1 year5 years10 years15 years20 years
Large-cap (S&P 500)65.2%76.3%84.3%89.5%92.0%
Mid-cap (S&P MidCap 400)62.0%80.0%77.3%87.5%90.9%
Small-cap (S&P SmallCap 600)29.7%60.4%82.2%90.7%90.8%

The figures are the shares of funds that lagged their index. The same report shows that only about 36% of the US stock funds that existed 20 years earlier survived to the end of 2024. In 2025, about 79% of active large-cap funds lagged the S&P 500 (SPIVA U.S. Scorecard, year-end 2025).

Check C2
In 2024 only about 30% of US active small-cap funds lagged the S&P SmallCap 600, but over 20 years about 91% lagged. The most reasonable reading of the 2024 result is:
If excess returns were easy in small caps, why do more than 80% lag over 10, 15 and 20 years?
The 1-year and 20-year figures come from the same report and the same method. The likely explanation lies in the funds and the index themselves.

The longer the horizon, the more funds lag

Section titled “The longer the horizon, the more funds lag”

One clear pattern in the table is that the longer the horizon, the larger the share of funds that lag. Suppose an active fund has no skill before costs, so its yearly excess return over the index averages −f-f−f (its cost), with a standard deviation equal to its tracking error σ\sigmaσ, independent and normally distributed from year to year. Its cumulative excess return over TTT years averages −fT-fT−fT with standard deviation σT\sigma\sqrt{T}σT​, so the probability that it beats the index over the TTT years is

P=N ⁣(−fTσ)P = N\!\left(-\frac{f\sqrt{T}}{\sigma}\right)P=N(−σfT​​)

N(⋅)N(\cdot)N(⋅) is the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution (normal distribution).

Check C3
In Figure 3-1, keep the cost at 1% and raise the tracking error from 5% to 10%. The probability that a fund with no skill beats the index over 20 years:
In the formula σ\sigmaσ is in the denominator. When σ\sigmaσ grows, does −fTσ-\frac{f\sqrt{T}}{\sigma}−σfT​​ move closer to 0 or further from it?
The average lag is indeed unchanged, but the probability also depends on how spread out the outcomes are. Look at the readout in the figure.

Persistence of performance

Section titled “Persistence of performance”

Even if most funds lag, perhaps investors can pick the ones that win? That requires persistence: funds that did well in the past keep doing well. The SPIVA Persistence Scorecard (year-end 2025) followed the 505 US stock funds in the top quarter by return in December 2021: by December 2025, not one had stayed in the top quarter in every following year. If rankings were purely random, the chance of staying in the top quarter 4 years in a row would be (14)4≈0.4%\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^4 \approx 0.4\%(41​)4≈0.4%, or about 2 funds. Of the 1,010 funds in the top half, 7.92% stayed in the top half for 4 years in a row, against (12)4=6.25%\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^4 = 6.25\%(21​)4=6.25% if random.

Check C4
For the SPIVA persistence result (none of 505 top-quarter funds stayed in the top quarter for 4 years in a row, against about 2 if random), the most reasonable conclusion is:
If rankings are mostly luck, this result appears without anyone "losing skill". What evidence could tell the two explanations apart?
If last year's ranking does not predict next year's, what does chasing the top fund each year achieve? What extra costs does it bring?

How to read fund documents

Section titled “How to read fund documents”

Choosing or evaluating a fund means reading its public documents:

  • The factsheet, usually updated monthly or quarterly, lists the expense ratio, size, inception date, benchmark, top ten holdings, sector and region breakdown, style box (large, mid or small cap × value, blend or growth), returns over various periods against the benchmark, and risk statistics: standard deviation, beta (beta), R2R^2R2 relative to the benchmark (R-squared), tracking error and Sharpe ratio.
  • The prospectus is a legal document. Its summary section at the front states the investment objective, the fee table (expense ratio), principal investment strategies, principal risks, past returns against an index, and the managers. The statement of additional information (SAI) has more detail, such as brokerage commissions and the managers’ own investment in the fund.
  • Annual and semiannual reports give the full holdings, financial statements and turnover (turnover ratio).

For active funds, one useful measure is active share: half the sum of the absolute differences between the fund’s weights and the benchmark’s weights (Cremers and Petajisto, 2009):

AS=12∑i∣wi−wiB∣AS = \frac{1}{2} \sum_i \left| w_{i} - w_{i}^{B} \right|AS=21​i∑​​wi​−wiB​​

wiw_iwi​ and wiBw_i^BwiB​ are the weights of stock iii in the fund and in the benchmark. An active share of 0 means the fund is identical to the benchmark; 100% means no overlap at all.

Check C5
An active large-cap fund has an expense ratio of 0.90%, an R2R^2R2 of 0.99 relative to the S&P 500 and an active share of 20%. The most reasonable judgment about this fund is:
R2R^2R2 measures the share of the fund's return explained by the index. What does 0.99 say about how different the fund's return is from the index?
Active share is computed from holdings weights; it measures how different the holdings are from the benchmark, not the return.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Before costs, active investors as a whole earn the market return; after costs, the average active dollar must lag passive investing.
  • The SPIVA reports show that most active funds lag their matching indexes, more so over longer horizons; liquidated funds are included.
  • The probability that a fund with no skill beats its index falls with the horizon, at a speed set by the ratio of cost to tracking error.
  • Funds ranked high in the past rarely stay high, and the results look much like random rankings.
  • Factsheets, prospectuses and annual reports give information on fees, strategy, risk and holdings; active share measures how different a fund is from its benchmark.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
Suppose 40% of the stock market's assets are held by index funds with a total cost of 0.05% a year, and 60% by active investors with an average total cost (fees and trading costs) of 0.80% a year.
(a) Weighted by money, do active investors earn more or less than the market after costs, and by how much?
(b) A fund manager says: "As passive investing grows, fewer people are looking for mispricing, so active investors as a group have a growing chance to beat the market." Evaluate this statement. Under what circumstances might "passive investors" earn something other than the market return even before costs?
Question 2
An intermediate core bond fund is benchmarked to the Bloomberg US Aggregate Bond Index. In 2024 it beat its benchmark by 0.6 percentage points. On average it held 20 percentage points more corporate bonds than the benchmark (and correspondingly fewer Treasuries), with the same interest rate risk (duration) as the benchmark; that year corporate bonds earned 2.5 percentage points more than Treasuries after removing the effect of rates.
(a) Roughly how much of the excess return came from the extra corporate bonds?
(b) The fund's marketing says: "Our managers beat the benchmark through excellent judgment." Evaluate this statement. In what kind of year would this approach lag the benchmark?
Question 3
Twenty years ago a fund company had 100 stock funds; 36 still exist and the rest were liquidated or merged. Of the 36 survivors, 25% beat their benchmarks over the 20 years.
(a) If none of the liquidated or merged funds beat its benchmark, what percentage of the original 100 funds beat their benchmarks?
(b) The company's advertisement says: "25% of our long-term funds beat their benchmarks, far better than the industry average." Evaluate this statement. Why are liquidated funds mostly poor performers?
Question 4
A "growth fund" factsheet shows: benchmark the S&P 500; over the past 10 years the fund returned 13% a year and the S&P 500 12%; the fund's beta is 1.2, its R2R^2R2 relative to the S&P 500 is 0.85, and its standard deviation 20% (15% for the S&P 500); expense ratio 0.75%. The risk-free rate averaged 2% over the period.
(a) By CAPM (4.4 The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)), what is the fund's Jensen alpha, roughly?
(b) The fund advertises that it "beats its benchmark by 1 percentage point a year". Evaluate this statement, and say what else should be looked at and against which benchmark.
